# Classification and Regression Trees (CART)

## Conceptual Overview

CART (Breiman et al., 1984) is a non-parametric supervised learning method that
**recursively partitions** the predictor space into rectangular regions. Each
partition is defined by a binary rule on a single predictor (e.g., `solar < 4200`).
The result is a tree structure where:

- **Internal nodes** contain split rules
- **Branches** represent the outcome of a rule (left = TRUE, right = FALSE)
- **Leaf nodes (terminal nodes)** contain predictions

Trees are grown **greedily** — at each node the algorithm considers every possible
split on every predictor and selects the one that maximally reduces impurity or
error. There is no backtracking.

**Key advantages for soil survey:**

| Property | Practical benefit |
|----------|------------------|
| Non-parametric | No distributional assumptions; handles skewed soil data |
| Mixed input types | Accepts numeric, categorical, and ordered-factor predictors |
| Handles missing values | Uses surrogate splits; no imputation needed |
| Interpretable | Single tree diagram readable by field pedologists |
| Covariate selection built-in | Only informative splits appear in the tree |

## Split Criteria

### Regression Trees — Residual Sum of Squares

For a **continuous** response (e.g., O horizon thickness `Otot`), CART minimises
the **Residual Sum of Squares (RSS)** at each candidate split $(j, t)$ — feature
$j$ cut at threshold $t$:

$$\Delta RSS = RSS_{\text{parent}} - \left[RSS_{\text{left}} + RSS_{\text{right}}\right]$$

where $RSS = \sum_{i \in \text{node}} (y_i - \bar{y}_{\text{node}})^2$.

The prediction at each leaf is the **mean** of the training samples in that leaf:

$$\hat{y}_{\text{leaf}} = \bar{y}_{\text{leaf}} = \frac{1}{N_{\text{leaf}}} \sum_{i \in \text{leaf}} y_i$$

**In R:** `rpart(y ~ x, method = "anova")`

### Classification Trees — Gini Impurity

For a **categorical** response (e.g., spodic intensity class, land cover), CART
minimises **node impurity**. The default is **Gini impurity**:

$$G = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k^2$$

where $p_k$ is the proportion of class $k$ samples at the node. A perfectly pure
node (all one class) has $G = 0$; maximum impurity (uniform distribution) has
$G = 1 - 1/K$.

**Entropy** (information gain, used by C4.5/ID3) is an alternative:

$$H = -\sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k \log_2(p_k)$$

The split that minimises the **weighted average** impurity of the two child nodes
is selected:

$$\text{Impurity}(j, t) = \frac{N_L}{N} G_L + \frac{N_R}{N} G_R$$

**Gini vs entropy in practice:** For most soil survey classification tasks, both
criteria produce nearly identical trees. Gini is computationally faster (no
logarithm). Entropy penalises near-pure nodes slightly more, which can sometimes
produce slightly deeper trees on multi-class problems.

**In R:** `rpart(y ~ x, method = "class")` (default: Gini)

### Multi-class vs Binary Classification

When the response has many classes (e.g., `spodint` with levels 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2),
CART must find splits that separate **five** distributions simultaneously. This is
harder than binary classification because:

1. Rare intermediate classes (0.5, 1.5) provide weak signal at any single threshold
2. Adjacent classes in an ordered factor are environmentally similar, blurring
   decision boundaries
3. The class imbalance problem compounds — the majority class dominates splits

**Collapsing to binary** (spodic / non-spodic) removes the ambiguous intermediate
boundaries. The pedological justification is that the spodic/non-spodic distinction
maps to a clear process threshold (illuviation of organic matter and Al/Fe oxides)
while the intermediate grades within spodic are more continuous.

> **Rule of thumb:** If cross-validation error is substantially lower for a binary
> model, the intermediate classes are not well-supported by the available covariates
> and may be better handled as a regression response or discarded for mapping purposes.

## Cost-Complexity Pruning

### The Overfitting Problem

A fully-grown tree (no `cp` constraint) will eventually place every training
observation in its own leaf — achieving zero training error but completely failing
on new data. This is **overfitting**: the model has memorised noise rather than
learned signal.

### The Cost-Complexity Criterion

`rpart` controls tree complexity through the **complexity parameter** $\alpha$
(`cp` in R). The cost-complexity criterion is:

$$R_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha \times |T|$$

where:

- $R(T)$ = training error (RSS for regression, misclassification rate for classification)
- $|T|$ = number of leaf nodes
- $\alpha$ = regularisation parameter (larger = simpler tree)

As $\alpha$ increases, the optimal tree gets smaller. `rpart` uses **10-fold
cross-validation** internally to estimate $R_\alpha(T)$ for a range of $\alpha$
values and records results in the `cptable`.

### Reading the CP Table

`printcp(model)` outputs:

| Column | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `CP` | Complexity parameter value for this row |
| `nsplit` | Number of splits in the tree at this CP |
| `rel error` | Training error relative to root node error |
| `xerror` | Cross-validation error (relative) |
| `xstd` | Standard error of `xerror` |

The **actual misclassification rate** for a classification tree is:
$$\text{error} = \text{Root Node Error} \times \text{xerror} \times 100\%$$

### The 1-SE Rule

Rather than always selecting the tree with the minimum `xerror`, the **1-SE rule**
(Breiman et al., 1984) selects the **simplest tree** whose CV error is within one
standard error of the minimum. This prefers interpretability:

$$\text{threshold} = \min(\text{xerror}) + \text{xstd at minimum}$$
$$\text{optimal CP} = \text{largest CP where } \text{xerror} \leq \text{threshold}$$

```r
cp_tbl  <- model$cptable
xerr    <- cp_tbl[, "xerror"]
xstd    <- cp_tbl[, "xstd"]
min_idx <- which.min(xerr)
thresh  <- xerr[min_idx] + xstd[min_idx]
cp_1se  <- cp_tbl[max(which(xerr <= thresh)), "CP"]
pruned  <- prune(model, cp = cp_1se)
```

> **Important:** Use `max(which(...))` not `min(which(...))` — you want the row
> with the **largest CP** (smallest tree) that is still within the threshold. The
> CP table is ordered from largest to smallest CP, so rows near the top are simpler
> trees.

### Visualising Pruning: `plotcp()`

`plotcp()` shows `xerror` (±1 SE) vs tree size. The horizontal dashed line marks
the 1-SE threshold. Any tree size below the line is a reasonable choice. Prefer
the leftmost (simplest) crossing point.

## Response Transformation: log1p for Skewed Data

### When to Transform

O horizon thickness (`Otot`) and many other soil properties are **right-skewed**:
the bulk of observations cluster near zero but a few extreme values (thick Histosol
O horizons, peaty inclusions) stretch the distribution far to the right. In a
regression tree:

1. The first split often isolates the outlier vs everything else, wasting the
   only top-level split
2. Node means are pulled toward outliers, distorting leaf predictions
3. RSS is dominated by the squared error on extreme observations

### The log1p Transform

$$y^* = \ln(1 + y)$$

`log1p()` rather than `log()` is used because it is defined at $y = 0$
($\log(1 + 0) = 0$), whereas $\log(0) = -\infty$.

The inverse (back-transform) is:

$$\hat{y} = e^{\hat{y}^*} - 1 = \text{expm1}(\hat{y}^*)$$

**Use `expm1()` rather than `exp() - 1`** to avoid catastrophic cancellation for
values near zero.

### Comparing Models on the Original Scale

Back-transformed predictions must be evaluated on the original scale for RMSE to
be interpretable in cm:

```r
pred_log_bt <- expm1(predict(model_log, newdata = val))
rmse_log    <- sqrt(mean((val$Otot - pred_log_bt)^2))
```

> **Caution:** The log1p transform does **not** always improve RMSE. If the outlier
> is also present in the validation set, the un-transformed model may perform worse
> even after back-transformation, because the extreme value is genuinely hard to
> predict. The real benefit of the transform is more stable splits and better
> generalisation across the bulk of the distribution.

# Random Forest

## Bagging: The Foundation

**Bootstrap AGGregating** (Breiman, 1996) is the principle underlying Random Forest:

1. Draw $B$ bootstrap samples from the training data (sampling with replacement,
   each sample $\approx 63\%$ of original data)
2. Fit a full decision tree $T_b$ to each sample
3. Average predictions across all trees:

$$\hat{f}_{\text{bag}}(x) = \frac{1}{B} \sum_{b=1}^{B} T_b(x)$$

For classification, use majority vote instead of averaging.

**Why does averaging work?**  For $B$ i.i.d. trees each with variance $\sigma^2$:

$$\text{Var}\!\left(\bar{T}\right) = \frac{\sigma^2}{B} \xrightarrow[B \to \infty]{} 0$$

But tree predictions are **correlated** (all trained on similar data), so the
actual variance reduction is:

$$\text{Var}\!\left(\hat{f}_{\text{bag}}\right) = \rho\,\sigma^2 + \frac{(1-\rho)\,\sigma^2}{B}$$

As $B \to \infty$, the second term vanishes but the first term $\rho\sigma^2$
remains — this is the irreducible bagging variance.

## Random Feature Subsampling: The RF Innovation

Breiman (2001) added one key modification: at **each split**, only a random
subset of `mtry` features is considered (not all features). This **decorrelates**
the trees, reducing $\rho$ toward zero and making the $\rho\sigma^2$ floor much
lower.

The result: Random Forest has strictly lower variance than bagging (all features
at every split).

## Key Parameters

### `ntree` — Number of Trees

More trees = more stable predictions. The OOB error should **plateau** as a
function of `ntree`. If the `plot(rf)` curve is still declining at your chosen
`ntree`, increase it.

- Typical range: 500–2000 for soil survey datasets
- For grid search: start with 500, increase after finding optimal `mtry`
- Computational cost scales linearly with `ntree`

### `mtry` — Features Tried per Split

Controls the degree of decorrelation:

| Setting | Effect |
|---------|--------|
| `mtry = 1` | Extreme randomisation; high bias, low variance |
| `mtry = p` | Equivalent to bagging; all features eligible |
| `mtry = sqrt(p)` | Breiman's default for classification |
| `mtry = p/3` | Breiman's default for regression |

For soil DSM with ~25 covariates ($p = 25$): default `mtry` ≈ 5 (classification)
or ≈ 8 (regression). Optimal `mtry` is data-dependent — use grid search.

**In R (`randomForest`):** `mtry = 5`  
**In R (`ranger`):** `mtry = 5`

### `nodesize` / `min.node.size` — Minimum Leaf Size

Controls tree depth. Larger values = shallower trees = more bias, less variance.

| Package | Argument | Default classification | Default regression |
|---------|----------|----------------------|-------------------|
| `randomForest` | `nodesize` | 1 | 5 |
| `ranger` | `min.node.size` | 1 | 5 |

For small soil survey datasets (n < 300), increasing `nodesize` to 5–10 often
helps prevent overfitting.

## Out-of-Bag (OOB) Error

Each bootstrap sample leaves out ~37% of observations (the **out-of-bag** sample).
Each tree predicts its own OOB observations. Aggregating these predictions across
all trees gives a **free cross-validation estimate** of generalisation error —
with no need for a separate hold-out set.

**Accessing OOB error:**

```r
# randomForest — regression
rf$mse[rf$ntree]       # final OOB MSE
rf$rsq[rf$ntree]       # final OOB R²
sqrt(rf$mse[rf$ntree]) # OOB RMSE

# randomForest — classification
rf$err.rate[rf$ntree, "OOB"]  # final OOB error rate

# ranger — any
sqrt(rf$prediction.error)  # OOB RMSE (regression) or error rate (classification)
```

> **Spatial caution:** OOB error assumes observations are independently drawn.
> For spatially-autocorrelated soil data, OOB error is **optimistic** — nearby
> training points can "leak" information across the bootstrap boundary. Always
> report spatially-blocked cross-validation for DSM deliverables.

## Variable Importance

### %IncMSE (Permutation Importance)

For each tree $b$ and each predictor $j$:

1. Obtain OOB predictions normally → baseline OOB MSE$_b$
2. **Randomly permute** predictor $j$ in the OOB data → permuted OOB MSE$_{b,j}$
3. Record the increase: $\text{MSE}_{b,j} - \text{MSE}_b$

Average across all trees:

$$\%\text{IncMSE}_j = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\frac{\text{MSE}_{b,j} - \text{MSE}_b}{\text{MSE}_b} \times 100$$

**Properties:**

- Unbiased with respect to predictor cardinality (number of categories)
- Can be negative (a predictor whose permutation actually reduces error — possible
  in small samples)
- Preferred for scientific inference and reporting

### IncNodePurity (Gini Importance)

Total RSS (regression) or Gini (classification) reduction attributable to splits 
on predictor $j$, summed across all nodes and all trees:

$$\text{IncNodePurity}_j = \sum_{b=1}^{B} \sum_{t: v(t)=j} \Delta\text{impurity}(t)$$

**Properties:**

- Fast to compute (recorded during tree-building, no re-evaluation needed)
- **Biased toward continuous predictors and high-cardinality categorical predictors**
  (more possible splits = more chances to accumulate importance)
- Useful for ranking but not for inferring the actual magnitude of effect

> **For soil survey publications:** use `%IncMSE` / `MeanDecreaseAccuracy` and
> note in methods that permutation importance was used. Avoid `IncNodePurity` /
> `MeanDecreaseGini` in conclusions about predictor strength.

## The Histosol Outlier Effect

A single extreme observation can inflate the OOB MSE and RSS, causing the model
to allocate many splits to separate it from the bulk of the data. This is detectable
by:

1. `hist(soildata$Otot)` — long right tail indicates a potential outlier
2. Comparing model performance with and without the observation
3. Large drop in MSE after removal confirms the observation was dominating the loss

**The pedological decision:** Histosols have a fundamentally different genesis
(peat accumulation) than the other soil orders in the dataset. If the mapping goal
is to predict O horizon thickness for mineral soils, removing Histosols is justified
and should be documented. If the goal includes Histosols, a separate model or a
Histosol presence/absence stratification may be more appropriate.

---

## Hyperparameter Tuning

### Grid Search

Exhaustive search over all combinations of hyperparameters:

```r
hyper_grid <- expand.grid(
  mtry     = c(3, 5, 8, 10),
  nodesize = c(1, 3, 5, 10),
  ntree    = c(200, 500, 1000)
)

for (i in seq_len(nrow(hyper_grid))) {
  model      <- randomForest(..., mtry = hyper_grid$mtry[i], ...)
  oob_err[i] <- model$err.rate[nrow(model$err.rate), "OOB"]
}
opt <- which.min(oob_err)
```

**Computational cost:** total models = $|\text{mtry}| \times |\text{nodesize}| \times |\text{ntree}|$.
For 4 × 4 × 3 = 48 combinations with `ntree = 500`, this is 24,000 trees.
Use `ranger` for grid search — 5–20× faster than `randomForest`.

### caret + ranger Tuning

`caret::train()` with `method = "ranger"` adds 10-fold CV to each hyperparameter
combination, giving a more reliable tuning estimate than OOB alone:

```r
tuning_grid <- expand.grid(
  mtry          = c(3, 5, 8),
  splitrule     = "variance",
  min.node.size = c(3, 5, 10)
)

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10, savePredictions = "final")

rf_tuned <- train(
  x = X, y = y,
  method    = "ranger",
  trControl = ctrl,
  tuneGrid  = tuning_grid,
  num.trees = 500
)

rf_tuned$bestTune   # optimal parameters
```

---

## randomForest vs ranger

| Feature | `randomForest` | `ranger` |
|---------|---------------|---------|
| Speed | Baseline | 5–20× faster (C++ parallelism) |
| OOB error access | `$err.rate[ntree, "OOB"]` | `$prediction.error` |
| Importance argument | `importance = TRUE` | `importance = "permutation"` |
| Parallel trees | `%dopar%` required | Built-in (`num.threads`) |
| Large datasets | Memory-limited | Handles large $n$, $p$ |
| `caret` integration | `method = "rf"` | `method = "ranger"` |

**Practical guidance:**

- Use `randomForest` for: exploratory work, `varImpPlot()`, `rfImpute()`
- Use `ranger` for: grid search, large DSM datasets, caret CV workflows
- Results should be numerically similar; minor differences from random seed

# Feature Selection with Boruta

## The Shadow Feature Approach

**Boruta** (Kursa & Rudnicki, 2010) is a wrapper around Random Forest that uses
a hypothesis-testing framework to classify each predictor as *Confirmed*,
*Tentative*, or *Rejected*.

**Algorithm:**

1. For each predictor $j$, create a **shadow copy** $j^*$ by randomly permuting
   its values (destroying any relationship with the response)
2. Create an augmented dataset with both original and shadow predictors ($2p$ features)
3. Fit a Random Forest on the augmented dataset and record `MeanDecreaseAccuracy`
   for all features
4. Compare each original predictor's importance against the **maximum** shadow
   importance (the `maxImp` benchmark)
5. Features significantly above `maxImp` → **Confirmed**; significantly below →
   **Rejected**; inconclusive → **Tentative**
6. Repeat (`maxRuns` iterations), accumulating the binomial test outcomes

**Key parameters:**

| Parameter | Default | Description |
|-----------|---------|-------------|
| `maxRuns` | 100 | Maximum RF iterations |
| `pValue` | 0.01 | Significance threshold for accept/reject |
| `doTrace` | 0 | Verbosity (0 = silent, 1 = basic, 2 = detailed) |

```r
fs_bor <- Boruta(y = y, x = X, maxRuns = 50, doTrace = 1)

# Extract confirmed features
vars_confirmed <- getSelectedAttributes(fs_bor)

# Resolve tentative features (optional)
vars_final <- getSelectedAttributes(TentativeRoughFix(fs_bor))

# Importance statistics per feature
attStats(fs_bor)[order(-attStats(fs_bor)$meanImp), ]
```

**Interpreting the plot:**

- **Green boxes:** Confirmed important (above max-shadow benchmark)
- **Yellow boxes:** Tentative (insufficient evidence to accept or reject)
- **Red boxes:** Rejected (consistently below max-shadow)
- **Blue boxes:** Shadow features (benchmarks)

> **Boruta vs manual feature selection:** Boruta is conservative — it accepts a
> feature only when there is strong statistical evidence of importance, not just
> correlation. For soil survey covariates derived from the same DEM (slope, aspect,
> TWI, etc.), highly correlated features often share the importance signal and
> Boruta may retain one while rejecting others. This is correct behaviour.

# Cross-Validation

## Why OOB Error Is Not Enough

OOB error assumes observations are drawn i.i.d. from the same population. Soil
survey pedons are **spatially structured** — nearby sites share geology, climate,
and land use. When the bootstrap sample contains sites 100 m from an OOB site,
the model sees nearly the same environmental signal in training and validation.
This produces **overly optimistic OOB error**.

**k-fold cross-validation** (k = 5 or 10) partitions the full dataset into $k$
groups, trains on $k-1$ and validates on 1, rotating until all observations have
been held out exactly once. Spatial CV further ensures that folds do not contain
nearby sites — critical for DSM and SSURGO update applications.

## 10-Fold CV with caret

The `caret::train()` function provides a standardised interface:

```r
tc <- trainControl(
  method          = "cv",
  number          = 10,
  returnResamp    = "all",       # save all fold predictions
  savePredictions = TRUE         # enables residual diagnostics
)

model_cv <- train(
  x          = X,               # predictor data frame
  y          = y,               # response vector
  method     = "ranger",        # or "rf", "rpart", etc.
  importance = "permutation",
  trControl  = tc
)

# Results
model_cv$results           # RMSE, R², MAE per parameter combo
model_cv$bestTune          # optimal parameters
model_cv$finalModel        # final model fit on ALL data with best params
```

**Metrics reported by caret:**

| Metric | Formula | Use |
|--------|---------|-----|
| RMSE | $\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}$ | Primary accuracy metric (original units) |
| R² (Rsquared) | $1 - \frac{\sum(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}{\sum(y_i - \bar{y})^2}$ | Proportion variance explained |
| MAE | $\frac{1}{n}\sum|y_i - \hat{y}_i|$ | Robust to outliers; interpretable in original units |

> **Log-scale models:** When the response was log1p-transformed, CV metrics from
> `caret` are on the **log scale**. To compare with un-transformed models, you must
> back-transform fold predictions manually or use a custom summary function.

# Confusion Matrix and Classification Evaluation

## Confusion Matrix Structure

A confusion matrix tabulates actual vs predicted classes. For binary classification:

|  | Predicted Positive | Predicted Negative |
|--|-------------------|-------------------|
| **Actual Positive** | True Positive (TP) | False Negative (FN) |
| **Actual Negative** | False Positive (FP) | True Negative (TN) |

`caret::confusionMatrix()` computes the matrix and a full suite of statistics:

```r
cm <- confusionMatrix(pred, reference, mode = "everything")
cm$overall    # Accuracy, Kappa, etc.
cm$byClass    # Sensitivity, Specificity, PPV, NPV, F1 per class
cm$table      # raw counts
```

## Key Metrics

### Overall Accuracy

$$\text{Accuracy} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN}$$

Proportion of all predictions that are correct. Misleading when classes are
imbalanced (a model predicting all non-spodic has high accuracy if 80% are
non-spodic).

### Cohen's Kappa

$$\kappa = \frac{P_o - P_e}{1 - P_e}$$

where $P_o$ = observed agreement, $P_e$ = expected agreement by chance.
$\kappa = 1$ = perfect, $\kappa = 0$ = no better than chance, $\kappa < 0$ = worse
than chance.

| $\kappa$ range | Interpretation |
|---------------|---------------|
| < 0.20 | Slight |
| 0.21–0.40 | Fair |
| 0.41–0.60 | Moderate |
| 0.61–0.80 | Substantial |
| > 0.80 | Almost perfect |

### Sensitivity and Specificity (Binary)

$$\text{Sensitivity (Recall)} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}$$
$$\text{Specificity} = \frac{TN}{TN + FP}$$

In soil survey context:

- **Sensitivity** = probability of correctly identifying a truly spodic site
  (producer's accuracy for the positive class)
- **Specificity** = probability of correctly identifying a truly non-spodic site

**Which matters more?** If the consequence of missing a spodic site (false
negative) is worse than over-mapping (false positive), optimise for sensitivity.
This is common in conservation-driven soil survey where under-mapping rare
features has regulatory consequences.

### F1 Score

$$F_1 = 2 \times \frac{\text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}$$

Harmonic mean of precision and recall. Useful for imbalanced classes where
overall accuracy is uninformative.

# Partial Dependence Plots

## Definition

A **Partial Dependence Plot (PDP)** shows the marginal effect of one or two
predictors on model predictions, averaging out the effect of all other predictors:

$$\hat{f}_{j}(x_j) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \hat{f}(x_j,\, \mathbf{x}_{-j,i})$$

For each value of $x_j$ in the plot, the model is evaluated for every observation
with that fixed value of $x_j$ and its actual other predictor values. The mean
prediction is plotted.

**Note:** PDPs assume **independence** between $x_j$ and $\mathbf{x}_{-j}$. When
predictors are correlated (e.g., elevation and temperature), the PDP may extrapolate
into unrealistic regions of predictor space. Accumulated Local Effects (ALE) plots
are a more robust alternative for correlated predictors.

## Using `pdp::partial()` with `ranger`

`purrr::partial()` masks `pdp::partial()` when both packages are loaded. Always
call explicitly:

```r
pdp1 <- pdp::partial(
  rf_final,
  pred.var       = "landsatb7",   # predictor to vary
  plot           = FALSE,          # return data frame, not plot
  grid.resolution = 30,            # number of unique values to evaluate
  train          = soildata        # needed for ranger models
)

ggplot(pdp1, aes(x = landsatb7, y = yhat)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2c5f2e", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_rug(data = soildata, aes(x = landsatb7, y = NULL),
           sides = "b", alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Landsat Band 7 Reflectance",
       y = "Partial Dependence (log1p O Horizon cm)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Back-transforming PDPs for log-scale models:**

```r
pdp1$yhat_cm <- expm1(pdp1$yhat)   # back to cm scale for interpretability
```

## 2-Way PDPs and Interaction Effects

```r
pdp_2way <- pdp::partial(
  rf_final,
  pred.var        = c("landsatb7", "solar"),
  grid.resolution = 20,
  plot            = TRUE,
  plot.engine     = "ggplot2",
  train           = soildata
)
```

A 2-way PDP reveals **interactions** — when the effect of one predictor changes
depending on the value of another. A flat surface indicates additivity; a curved
or twisted surface indicates interaction.

---

# Model Evaluation Framework

## Regression Models: Selecting the Best

For O horizon thickness models, compare:

| Model | Error metric | Scale |
|-------|-------------|-------|
| rpart full (raw) | Validation RMSE | cm |
| rpart pruned (raw) | Validation RMSE | cm |
| rpart pruned (log1p, back-transformed) | Validation RMSE | cm |
| RF raw (Histosol removed) | OOB RMSE | cm |
| RF log1p (back-transformed) | OOB RMSE | cm |

> **Comparing OOB vs validation RMSE:** OOB and hold-out RMSE are computed on
> different subsets and by different mechanisms. They are comparable in magnitude
> but should not be directly subtracted to infer improvement. All models should
> ideally be evaluated on the same held-out test set.

## Classification Models: Multi-Class vs Binary

| Metric | Multi-class spodint | Binary spodic/non-spodic |
|--------|--------------------|-----------------------|
| Overall accuracy | Lower | Higher |
| Kappa | Lower | Higher |
| Misclassification rate | `Root Node Error × xerror` | `Root Node Error × xerror` |
| Practical mapping use | Intensity gradient map | Presence/absence map |

The binary model's higher accuracy does not mean it is always preferable. If
the objective is to distinguish between low-spodic and high-spodic sites for
management, the multi-class model provides information that the binary model
discards.

## Diagnostic Plots

### Observed vs Predicted (1:1 plot)

```r
plot(observed, predicted, pch = 16, col = "#2c5f2e",
     xlab = "Observed Otot (cm)", ylab = "Predicted Otot (cm)")
abline(0, 1, col = "red", lwd = 2)  # perfect prediction line
```

Systematic bias appears as a cloud above (underprediction) or below (overprediction)
the 1:1 line.

### Residual Diagnostics

```r
residuals <- observed - predicted

plot(predicted, residuals, pch = 16)    # heteroscedasticity check
abline(h = 0, col = "red")

qqnorm(residuals)                        # normality check
qqline(residuals, col = "red")
```

A funnel-shaped residual plot (variance increasing with predicted value) is a
common signature of a skewed response that benefits from log transformation.

# Spatial Prediction Workflow

## Standard Pipeline

```
Environmental covariates (rasters)
       ↓
Coregister to common CRS, resolution, extent (terra/raster)
       ↓
Stack into SpatRaster (terra::rast())
       ↓
Rename layers to match model predictor names exactly
       ↓
terra::predict(raster_stack, fitted_model, type = "response")
       ↓
Back-transform if response was log1p-transformed
       ↓
terra::writeRaster() → .tif for GIS
```

## Naming Convention

```r
names(raster_stack) == names(coef(model))[-1]  # must match exactly
```

`terra::predict()` matches raster layer names to model predictor names. Any
mismatch causes an error. If your raster files have different names than the
column names in training data, rename either the layers or the model covariates.

## Probability vs Class Maps

| Output type | `type = ` | Units | Use case |
|-------------|----------|-------|---------|
| Class map | `"response"` | Factor (class label) | Final map product |
| Probability map | `"prob"` | 0–1 per class | Uncertainty, threshold-based mapping |
| Vote count | `"vote"` | Integer per class | Ensemble inspection |

**Thresholding probability maps:** Rather than using majority vote (implicit in
`type = "response"`), you can apply a custom threshold to the probability surface
to trade off sensitivity vs specificity:

```r
LC_prob_spodic <- LC_prob[["spodic"]]     # probability of spodic class
LC_thresh      <- LC_prob_spodic > 0.4    # classify as spodic if P > 0.4
```

Lowering the threshold increases sensitivity (fewer missed spodic sites) at the
cost of specificity (more non-spodic sites classified as spodic).

# Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|-----------|
| **OOB error** | Out-of-bag error; free internal validation estimate in RF |
| **mtry** | Number of predictor candidates evaluated at each split |
| **nodesize / min.node.size** | Minimum observations required to split a node |
| **CP (complexity parameter)** | Regularisation term in rpart pruning |
| **1-SE rule** | Select simplest tree within 1 SE of minimum CV error |
| **Gini impurity** | Node impurity measure for classification: $1 - \sum p_k^2$ |
| **%IncMSE** | Permutation importance: increase in OOB MSE when predictor is shuffled |
| **IncNodePurity** | Gini/RSS reduction importance (biased; use %IncMSE for inference) |
| **Bagging** | Bootstrap aggregating: average many trees to reduce variance |
| **Decorrelation** | RF's `mtry` trick to reduce inter-tree correlation and further reduce variance |
| **log1p transform** | $\ln(1 + y)$; stabilises variance in right-skewed responses |
| **expm1** | $e^x - 1$; exact inverse of log1p; use instead of `exp(x) - 1` |
| **Boruta** | RF-based feature selection using shadow-feature hypothesis testing |
| **PDP** | Partial Dependence Plot; marginal effect of one predictor |
| **Spatial CV** | Cross-validation with geographically blocked folds |
| **DSM** | Digital Soil Mapping; spatial prediction of soil properties using covariates |
| **CLORPT** | Jenny's five soil-forming factors: Climate, Organisms, Relief, Parent material, Time |
